Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Renewable energy sources play an increasingly important role in the global energy mix, as the effort to reduce the environmental impact of energy production increases.

Out of all the renewable energy alternatives, wind energy is one of the most developed technologies worldwide. The U.S Department of Energy has put together a guide to achieving operational efficiency using predictive maintenance practices.

Predictive maintenance uses sensor information and analysis methods to measure and predict degradation and future component capability. The idea behind predictive maintenance is that failure patterns are predictable and if component failure can be predicted accurately and the component is replaced before it fails, the costs of operation and maintenance will be much lower.

The sensors fitted across different machines involved in the process of energy generation collect data related to various environmental factors (temperature, humidity, wind speed, etc.) and additional features related to various parts of the wind turbine (gearbox, tower, blades, break, etc.).

Objective¶

“ReneWind” is a company working on improving the machinery/processes involved in the production of wind energy using machine learning and has collected data of generator failure of wind turbines using sensors. They have shared a ciphered version of the data, as the data collected through sensors is confidential (the type of data collected varies with companies). Data has 40 predictors, 20000 observations in the training set and 5000 in the test set.

The objective is to build various classification models, tune them, and find the best one that will help identify failures so that the generators could be repaired before failing/breaking to reduce the overall maintenance cost. The nature of predictions made by the classification model will translate as follows:

  • True positives (TP) are failures correctly predicted by the model. These will result in repairing costs.
  • False negatives (FN) are real failures where there is no detection by the model. These will result in replacement costs.
  • False positives (FP) are detections where there is no failure. These will result in inspection costs.

It is given that the cost of repairing a generator is much less than the cost of replacing it, and the cost of inspection is less than the cost of repair.

“1” in the target variables should be considered as “failure” and “0” represents “No failure”.

Use:

-Primary Metric: Recall -Secondary Metric: F1 Score or Precision

Because the most expensive mistake in this problem is:

-False Negative (FN) → the model misses a real generator failure → leads to generator replacement cost, downtime, operational disruption, and possibly safety risk.

The business statement explicitly says:

-Replacement cost >> Repair cost >> Inspection cost

So the priority is:

  1. Detect as many actual failures as possible
  2. Even if it causes some extra inspections or repairs

Mathematically, Recall focuses exactly on minimizing False Negatives:

F1 Score is useful because it balances Recall and Precision:

This helps ensure the model does not create an excessive number of false alarms while still capturing failures.

⸻

Data Description¶

The data provided is a transformed version of the original data which was collected using sensors.

  • Train.csv - To be used for training and tuning of models.
  • Test.csv - To be used only for testing the performance of the final best model.

Both the datasets consist of 40 predictor variables and 1 target variable.

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Univariate analysis¶

In [127]:
# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.

def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to the show density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram
In [128]:
for feature in data.columns:
    histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None)

Observations from Univariate Analysis¶

  1. All variables are in +/- numbers under 15. This suggests that the features are likely standardized or scaled, which is a good practice for neural networks, and explicit normalization may not be required if the ranges are already consistent.
  2. Outliers should not be removed. In predictive maintenance, outliers often represent critical events, such as anomalies or early signs of failure. Removing them would mean discarding valuable information that is crucial for detecting and predicting equipment malfunctions.

Observation on Target Variable Distribution¶

  • Class Imbalance: Both the training and test datasets exhibit a significant class imbalance. The 'Target' variable (representing 'failure' or 'no failure') shows that the 'no failure' class (0) constitutes approximately 94.45% of the training data and 94.36% of the test data. Conversely, the 'failure' class (1) represents a much smaller proportion, about 5.55% in the training data and 5.64% in the test data. This indicates that failure events are rare, which is typical in predictive maintenance scenarios. It is crucial to address this imbalance during model training to prevent the model from becoming biased towards the majority class and failing to accurately predict the minority (failure) class.

Observations from Bivariate Analysis (Correlation Heatmap)¶

  1. Feature Inter-correlations: Many features show moderate to strong correlations with each other. For example, V12 and V13 appear to be highly positively correlated, and V15 and V16 are also strongly correlated. This suggests potential multicollinearity among the predictor variables, which might be a consideration for certain models, but for neural networks, it is generally less of a concern due to their ability to learn complex relationships.
  2. Correlation with Target Variable: Several features exhibit varying degrees of correlation with the Target variable. Features like V3, V12, V13, V18, V19, V24, V26, V32, V35, and V36 show some positive correlation, while V1, V2, V6, V7, V11, V14, V15, V16, V21, V28, V29, V34, V38, and V40 show some negative correlation. These correlations, even if subtle, indicate that these features contribute to predicting generator failure.
  3. No Extremely High Correlations with Target: While some features show correlations with the target, none appear to have an extremely high linear correlation (close to 1 or -1). This is typical for real-world predictive maintenance datasets, where failures are often complex and depend on a combination of factors rather than a single dominant one.

Overall, the heatmap provides a good visual summary of the linear relationships within the dataset, highlighting potential feature dependencies and indicating which features might be more influential in predicting the target variable.

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

In the predictive maintenance application, the primary business objective is to minimize the risk of missing actual generator failures. Since generator replacement and operational downtime carry significantly higher costs than inspections or preventive repairs, the model evaluation focuses primarily on Recall to maximize failure detection capability.

Recall is the most important metric because it directly measures the model’s ability to identify true failure events while minimizing False Negatives. A missed failure can result in unexpected equipment breakdown, operational disruption, safety concerns, and substantial financial impact to the business.

While maximizing Recall is critical, the model must also maintain reasonable Precision to avoid generating excessive false alarms. High false positive rates can lead to unnecessary inspections, maintenance activity, and inefficient resource allocation across maintenance operations.

To balance these competing objectives, F1 Score is used as a secondary evaluation metric because it combines both Recall and Precision into a single performance measure. This ensures the model maintains strong failure detection capability while still controlling operational inefficiencies caused by overprediction.

Utility Functions

In [350]:
def plot(history, name):
    """
    Function to plot loss/accuracy

    history: an object which stores the metrics and losses.
    name: can be one of Loss or Accuracy
    """
    fig, ax = plt.subplots() #Creating a subplot with figure and axes.
    plt.plot(history.history[name]) #Plotting the train accuracy or train loss
    plt.plot(history.history['val_'+name]) #Plotting the validation accuracy or validation loss

    plt.title('Model ' + name.capitalize()) #Defining the title of the plot.
    plt.ylabel(name.capitalize()) #Capitalizing the first letter.
    plt.xlabel('Epoch') #Defining the label for the x-axis.
    fig.legend(['Train', 'Validation'], loc="outside right upper") #Defining the legend, loc controls the position of the legend.
In [351]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using statsmodels
def model_performance_classification(
    model, predictors, target, threshold=0.5
):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    threshold: threshold for classifying the observation as class 1
    """

    # checking which probabilities are greater than threshold
    pred = model.predict(predictors) > threshold
    # pred_temp = model.predict(predictors) > threshold
    # # rounding off the above values to get classes
    # pred = np.round(pred_temp)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred, average='macro')  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1 Score": f1,}, index = [0]
    )

    return df_perf

         1.0       0.98      0.85      0.91       777

    accuracy                           0.99     14000
   macro avg       0.99      0.93      0.95     14000
weighted avg       0.99      0.99      0.99     14000
  • It is extremely strong at predicting “No Failure”
  • It is reasonably good at predicting failures
  • It is still missing some failures

Recall = 0.85

This is the key metric for my problem.

It means:

  • the model catches 85% of real generator failures
  • but misses about 15% of failures

Those missed failures become:

  • expensive replacements,
  • downtime,
  • maintenance risk.

So this is good, but should be improved

Accuracy is misleading here because the dataset is imbalanced.

We have:

  • 13,223 normal cases
  • only 777 failures

So the model can get high accuracy mainly by predicting the majority class correctly.

For predictive maintenance: Recall and F1 are more important than Accuracy.

Model 1, with its added layers, shows a slight improvement in detecting generator failures, increasing Recall from 0.83 to 0.85, and F1-score from 0.89 to 0.90 on the validation set, compared to Model 0. This indicates a better balance between identifying failures and controlling false alarms, making it a step forward in our predictive maintenance strategy.

Model 2: Increasing hidden layers and adding drop out¶

Introduce Regularization, Add drop out Rate of 50% after the first hidden layer. Add one more hidden layer, start from 256, 128, 64

In [383]:
# clears the current Keras session, resetting all layers and models previously created, freeing up memory and resources.
tf.keras.backend.clear_session()
In [384]:
#Initializing the neural network for Model 2
model_2 = Sequential()
model_2.add(Dense(256, activation="relu", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))
model_2.add(Dropout(0.5)) # Drop out rate
model_2.add(Dense(128, activation="relu", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))
model_2.add(Dense(64, activation="relu", input_dim=X_train.shape[1]))
model_2.add(Dense(1, activation="sigmoid"))

Model 2, with additional layers and dropout, further improves failure detection. Validation Recall increased to 0.87 (from 0.85 in Model 1), and the F1-score rose to 0.92 (from 0.90 in Model 1). This signifies a better ability to identify impending generator failures while maintaining high precision (0.98), minimizing false alarms. This model represents a strong step forward in our predictive maintenance strategy, balancing effective failure detection with operational efficiency.

Slight indication of diminishing returns / mild over-regularization
* Network is already fairly large:
    * 256 → 128 → 64
    * with 50% dropout
Yet validation metrics are almost unchanged from simpler models.

As we have are dealing with an imbalance in class distribution, we should also be using class weights to allow the model to give proportionally more importance to the minority class

from sklearn.utils import class_weight
import numpy as np

# Calculate class weights for imbalanced dataset

    class_weight='balanced',
    classes=np.unique(y_train),
    y=y_train
)

# Create a dictionary mapping class indices to their respective class weights
class_weights_dict = dict(enumerate(class_weights))
print("Class Weights:", class_weights_dict)

Model 4, employing the Adam optimizer, exhibited significant overfitting on the validation set, indicated by diverging loss curves. While achieving a validation F1-score of 0.92, its reduced generalizability makes it less suitable than Model 3 for reliable failure prediction.

Model 5, with class weights and Adam optimizer, achieves a validation Recall of 0.939 and an F1-score of 0.938. This shows improved Recall over Model 1, slightly higher Recall but lower F1-score than Model 2, comparable performance to Model 3, and significantly outperforms Model 4 in generalizability and metrics.

Model 6: Using Adam Optimizer and Dropout with balanced class weights¶

In [431]:
from sklearn.utils import class_weight
import numpy as np

# Calculate class weights for imbalanced dataset
class_weights = class_weight.compute_class_weight(
    class_weight='balanced',
    classes=np.unique(y_train),
    y=y_train
)

# Create a dictionary mapping class indices to their respective class weights
class_weights_dict = dict(enumerate(class_weights))
print("Class Weights:", class_weights_dict)

From the validation set performance comparison:

  • Model 5 emerged as a strong candidate, with Recall of 0.939 and F1-score of 0.938. This is a significant improvement over Model 0, 1, 2 and even Model 3's 0.942 Recall and 0.937 F1-score, making it a highly effective model for minimizing undetected failures.
  • Model 6 achieved Recall of 0.941 and F1-score of 0.934. While slightly higher in Recall than Model 5, its F1-score is marginally lower. However, it still shows robustness, good generalization, and limited overfitting.
  • Model 3 achieved a Recall of 0.942 and F1-score of 0.937, making it competitive.
  • Model 4 shows a strong Recall (0.932) and F1-score (0.924) on the validation set, but the previous analysis indicated significant overfitting on the training data, making it less reliable for generalization.
  • Model 0, Model 1, and Model 2 demonstrate progressively improving Recall and F1-score values (from Model 0's Recall 0.913, F1 0.943 to Model 2's Recall 0.934, F1 0.959). These models show consistent learning, but are outperformed by Models 3, 5, and 6 in terms of Recall, which is our primary metric.

Final Model Recommendation¶

Considering the primary objective to maximize Recall (to minimize undetected failures, which lead to expensive replacements) and also taking into account the F1-score for a balanced performance, Model 3 is the recommended model.

Reasoning:

  • Highest Recall (0.942): Model 3 achieved the highest Recall on the validation set among all models (0.942). This is crucial for ReneWind, as it directly addresses the most expensive mistake: missing actual generator failures. Model 6 had a very similar Recall (0.941) and Model 5 had a Recall of 0.939, but Model 3 slightly edges them out on this critical metric.
  • Strong F1-score (0.937): Along with the highest Recall, Model 3 also demonstrates a strong F1-score of 0.937. This indicates a good balance between Precision and Recall, ensuring that while we are catching most true failures, we are not generating an excessive number of false alarms (inspections).
  • Robustness to Overfitting: Unlike Model 4, which showed signs of significant overfitting despite a decent validation F1-score, Model 3, with its use of class weights and dropout, maintained a healthy relationship between training and validation losses, suggesting good generalization capabilities.
  • Efficient Training Time: Model 3's training time was approximately 53 seconds, which is competitive and more efficient than models like Model 5 (65 seconds) and Model 6 (66 seconds) that offered comparable or slightly lower performance on the key metrics.

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

The model achieved strong overall classification performance on the test dataset, with high Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score. This indicates that the model has learned meaningful patterns from the data and performs reliably on unseen observations.

The close alignment between Precision and Recall suggests a balanced classifier with effective control of both false positives and false negatives. This balance is important in machine learning applications where both detection capability and prediction reliability matter.

The model demonstrated strong minority class prediction performance despite class imbalance in the dataset. High Recall indicates that the classifier effectively captures positive cases rather than favoring the majority class.

The stable test performance relative to training results suggests good generalization capability with limited signs of overfitting. The model appears to maintain predictive consistency across different data samples.

The loss curve behavior indicates stable convergence during training, with validation loss remaining controlled throughout the learning process. This suggests that the optimization process was effective and the model architecture is reasonably well tuned.

Further improvements can focus on hyperparameter optimization, threshold tuning, and cross-validation to improve robustness and deployment reliability. Additional experimentation with regularization, class balancing techniques, and architecture refinement may further enhance minority class prediction performance.

Recommendations

The selected predictive maintenance model demonstrates strong overall classification performance, achieving high Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score on the test dataset, indicating effective identification of potential equipment failures while maintaining low false alarm rates. The balanced Precision-Recall performance suggests the model can reliably detect failure conditions without excessively misclassifying healthy equipment, which is critical in maintenance optimization applications.

Model reliably captures true failures while minimizing false negatives and false positives. This model can be used in productoon, it will help optimize business costs by using predictive maintence approach, for equipment repair and replacement as appropriate. This will also reduce business risk by minimizing false negatives.

Additional dataset, for training and testing, with higher representation of minority class (Failure) would help improve on this model and improve both primary and secondary metrics.
